title: In 1586, 40 capstans sharing the load by themselves moved the 327-tonne Vatican obelisk
body: In 1586 Pope Sixtus V had the Vatican obelisk, a 25.3 m needle of red granite brought from Egypt under Emperor Caligula, moved from beside St Peter’s Basilica to the middle of the square in front of it. It is the only obelisk in Rome that has stood since Roman times without falling. The architect Domenico Fontana first worked out its weight: a cubic palm of the same stone (a Roman palm is about 22 cm) weighed 86 pounds, and the shaft held about 11,204 of them, so **963,537 pounds**, some 327 tonnes. One capstan, an upright drum turned by men and horses, could lift about 20,000 pounds, so he used 40, plus five huge levers. Critics said the capstans could never pull together. Fontana knew that four horses could not break one of his ropes, so an overloaded capstan would simply stop turning while the slacker ones caught up: **they shared the load by themselves**. A trumpet meant turn and a bell meant stop. On 30 April 907 men and 75 horses lifted it; on 10 September 800 men and 140 horses raised it in its new place, as [Fontana’s own book of 1590](https://archive.org/details/gri_33125008662708) records. The story of a sailor who shouted ‘water on the ropes’ is a later legend.

slides.question: On 30 April 1586, how many men worked Domenico Fontana’s 40 capstans and five levers to lift the Vatican obelisk?
slides.explanation: 907 men and 75 horses, Fontana wrote in his 1590 book. In 12 moves they lifted the obelisk 2¾ palms, about 61 cm, so a sledge could be slid under it.

slides.alt: Animation in the style of an old engraving: the Vatican obelisk beside St Peter's in 1586; a cubic palm of granite on a steelyard; a capstan turned by a horse; a timber tower round the obelisk; 40 ropes that snap in a cascade, then share the load; the obelisk lifted, rolled and raised at sunset.
slides.music: “Send for the Horses” Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com) · CC BY 4.0

slides.prompt: Make the ropes start at least half uneven, choose what an overloaded rope does, and sound the trumpet until the obelisk is up 2¾ palms with no rope snapped.
slides.takeaway: If an overloaded rope snaps, its load jumps to the others and they snap in turn. If its capstan just stops, the slacker ones keep turning until they take their share, as Fontana argued: no rope breaks.

slides.alt: Photo of the Vatican obelisk in the middle of St Peter’s Square: a tall plain pink-granite shaft with a cross on top, standing on bronze lions and a stone pedestal, between curved colonnades, with the long street to the Tiber behind it under a cloudy blue sky.

slides.question: Domenico Fontana’s critics feared one of his 40 capstans would take all the obelisk’s weight and break. Why didn’t it?
options: A gear kept all 40 in step
The levers took the extra weight
slides.explanation: Four horses could not break one of his ropes, so an overloaded capstan just couldn’t turn, while the slacker ones kept turning until they took their share.
